text: How do HTML, CSS, and JavaScript work together when a browser displays an interactive web page?
key_points: HTML describes content and structure|CSS controls presentation and layout|JavaScript adds behavior and updates the DOM|browser combines these resources to render the page

text: What happens when someone submits an HTML form, and how would you make its fields easy to use?
key_points: named controls contribute values to the submission|action and method determine the request destination and method|labels and keyboard access help people use the fields|client validation helps usability but the server must validate too

text: How would you explain the CSS box model and work out how much space an element occupies?
key_points: content is surrounded by padding and border|margin separates the element from its neighbors|content-box width excludes padding and border|border-box width includes padding and border but not margin

text: How do a browser and a web server exchange information when someone opens a page or submits an action?
key_points: client sends a request to a resource URL|request carries a method and headers and sometimes a body|server returns a status code and headers and sometimes a body|browser uses the response to render or update the interface

text: Why would you choose meaningful HTML elements instead of building an entire page from generic containers?
key_points: elements communicate the meaning of content|headings and landmarks help navigation|native controls provide built-in keyboard behavior|semantic structure helps assistive technology and maintenance

text: How would you check whether a navigation menu and a form are usable without a mouse?
key_points: test navigation and activation using the keyboard|keep focus order logical and focus visibly indicated|controls need accessible names and forms need associated labels|avoid focus traps and expose validation errors accessibly

text: Two CSS rules assign different colors to the same element. How would you determine which declaration takes effect?
key_points: check whether each selector matches and the rule applies|cascade compares origin importance and layers before specificity|specificity resolves competing declarations at the same cascade level|source order resolves a remaining tie

text: How do Flexbox and Grid differ, and how would you decide which to use for a particular layout?
key_points: Flexbox primarily arranges items along one axis|Grid coordinates rows and columns together|choose based on the relationships the layout must preserve|they can be combined for page layout and component alignment

text: What makes a web page responsive, and how would you test its behavior on narrow and wide screens?
key_points: use flexible layouts and appropriately sized media|adapt layout with media queries where content needs a change|configure the viewport for mobile rendering|test overflow readability and interactions at several widths

text: What is a closure in JavaScript, and why can a function still use a variable after its outer function has returned?
key_points: a function retains access to its lexical environment|captured bindings remain available while the closure is reachable|useful for callbacks and private state|captured mutable bindings are not frozen copies of their values

text: How do JavaScript equality comparisons behave for primitive values and for two separately created objects?
key_points: strict equality does not perform type coercion|loose equality may convert operand types|objects compare by identity rather than matching properties|compare relevant fields explicitly when value equality is needed

text: How do promises and async functions help handle an HTTP request, and how should failures be handled?
key_points: a promise represents a future fulfillment or rejection|await suspends the async function without blocking the main thread|handle rejected promises with catch or try and catch|fetch does not reject just because an HTTP response is an error status

text: Why can a long JavaScript calculation make a page unresponsive even while network requests are handled asynchronously?
key_points: a running JavaScript job completes before another job executes|long work on the main thread delays input and rendering|asynchronous I/O does not make synchronous calculation nonblocking|split the work or move suitable computation to a worker

text: How can one event handler respond to clicks on a list whose items are added dynamically?
key_points: use event delegation on a stable ancestor|bubbling brings applicable child events to the ancestor|inspect the target or closest matching element|distinguish target from currentTarget and check the element belongs to the list

text: How would you choose an HTTP method for an API operation, and why does its retry behavior matter?
key_points: GET should retrieve information without requesting a state change|POST commonly processes or creates data and is not inherently idempotent|PUT and DELETE have idempotent intended effects|retries need to preserve application intent rather than duplicate side effects

text: What information should an API return when a request succeeds, contains invalid input, or fails unexpectedly?
key_points: choose a status code that describes the outcome|successful responses return a documented representation or no body as appropriate|client errors should describe actionable validation or access problems|server errors should not expose stack traces or private data

text: How can a browser reuse a cached response while still checking whether the resource has changed?
key_points: Cache-Control governs freshness and allowed reuse|ETag or Last-Modified can act as a validator|conditional requests can receive 304 when the cached representation is still valid|no-cache requires validation whereas no-store forbids storage

text: An API request works in a command-line client but the browser cannot read its response. How would you investigate?
key_points: compare the page origin with the API origin|inspect browser console and network details for CORS failures|check allowed origins and any required preflight method or headers|CORS controls browser access to responses and does not replace server authentication

text: How can a server recognize a signed-in user across multiple requests, and how should the browser credential be protected?
key_points: a session credential links requests to server-side identity or verified claims|protect transport with HTTPS and restrict credential lifetime|HttpOnly limits script access to a cookie and Secure restricts it to secure transport|SameSite and CSRF defenses address unwanted cross-site credential use

text: How do authentication and authorization differ, and where should access to a protected resource be checked?
key_points: authentication establishes who is making the request|authorization checks what that identity may do|enforce permissions on the server for each protected operation|hiding a control in the browser is not an access-control check

text: What can go wrong when a web page renders text supplied by another user, and how would you prevent it?
key_points: untrusted content can execute script if interpreted as markup or code|use text rendering or context-appropriate output encoding|sanitize with a suitable allowlist when rich HTML is necessary|content security policy is defense in depth rather than a substitute for safe rendering

text: Why might a cookie-authenticated application need protection against requests initiated by another website?
key_points: the browser can attach session cookies to attacker-triggered requests|a state-changing endpoint may act as the signed-in victim|validate an anti-CSRF token and appropriate request-origin signals|SameSite can reduce exposure but is not a universal replacement for CSRF defenses

text: Why is constructing a database query by concatenating user input risky, and how should the query be built instead?
key_points: input can change the structure of a SQL statement|parameterized queries separate data from query syntax|validate input but do not rely on validation alone|dynamic identifiers need an allowlist rather than ordinary value parameters

text: How can a database index help a web application, and what costs would you consider before adding one?
key_points: an appropriate index can avoid scanning all rows|choose indexes based on filters joins and ordering in actual queries|indexes consume storage and add work to writes|inspect query plans and measure rather than assuming every query improves

text: A page looks correct on a laptop but scrolls horizontally on a phone. How would you find and fix the cause?
key_points: reproduce at a narrow viewport and locate the overflowing element|inspect fixed widths minimum sizes padding and media dimensions|adjust the responsible layout constraint rather than hiding all overflow|retest content and interactions at several widths

text: A search box sometimes shows results for an older query after the user types a newer one. How would you fix it?
key_points: requests can finish in a different order from their creation|apply a result only if its request still matches the latest query|cancel superseded requests where possible and handle cancellation|test delayed and out-of-order responses rather than relying on debouncing alone

text: An API listing a customer's orders becomes slow as the database grows. How would you investigate and improve it?
key_points: measure where request time is spent and inspect the executed queries|check query plans and indexes matching the customer filter and ordering|limit returned data with pagination and avoid repeated per-row queries|verify the improvement with representative data and preserve authorization checks

text: A comment feature must display user text and optionally a small amount of formatting. How would you implement it safely?
key_points: render plain comments as text rather than raw HTML|define which formatting is allowed before accepting rich content|use a maintained sanitizer for permitted markup and safe URL schemes|test hostile markup and use content security policy as an additional layer

text: An order submission times out and the user retries, creating two orders. How would you prevent that without losing a valid retry?
key_points: a timeout does not prove the first request failed|reuse an idempotency key for retries of the same intended operation|atomically associate the key and request with the result on the server|return the original result on a matching retry and reject conflicting reuse

text: A signed-in user changes an order ID in a URL and sees another user's order. How would you investigate and fix this?
key_points: identify a missing object-level permission check|scope the server query or check access against the authenticated identity|do not trust a client-supplied owner or rely on hard-to-guess identifiers|test access by the owner another user and an unauthenticated client
